title: The Courthouse at Lancaster
subtitle: The Haudenosaunee (Six Nations) council with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia, Lancaster, Pennsylvania, June–July 1744
intro: For thirteen days in the summer of 1744 the brick courthouse of Lancaster, a German and Scots-Irish market town some sixty miles west of Philadelphia, held the largest Indian council the English colonies had yet staged. Deputies of the Haudenosaunee (Six Nations, "Iroquois") Confederacy, led by the Onöñda'gega' (Onondaga) speaker Canasatego, met Governor George Thomas of Pennsylvania and commissioners from Virginia and Maryland. The two southern colonies wanted the Confederacy's claims to land inside their charters extinguished; the Haudenosaunee wanted payment for lands already settled without purchase, an end to clashes with Virginians on the warriors' path south, and the alliance called the Covenant Chain kept bright. War between Britain and France had just been declared, and every party knew it.

The background is the Philadelphia council of July 1742, where Canasatego complained that settlers from the south were living on unpurchased Haudenosaunee land west of the Susquehanna, and where he ordered the Lenape (Delaware) off the Forks of the Delaware in support of Pennsylvania's disputed Walking Purchase. A violent encounter between a Haudenosaunee war party and Virginia militia in the Shenandoah Valley that December made a settlement urgent; the interpreter Conrad Weiser carried Virginia's overtures to Onondaga in July 1743, with the botanist John Bartram in his company, and the meeting at Lancaster was the result.

Almost all of the written record was made by the colonial side. The official minutes, printed by Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia in 1744 and attested by the Pennsylvania secretary Richard Peters, set down the Haudenosaunee speeches only as Conrad Weiser rendered them into English; no Haudenosaunee-authored text of the council survives, and the Confederacy's own record was kept in wampum and memory. Beside the minutes stand the private journal of Witham Marshe, secretary to the Maryland commissioners (first printed in 1801), Franklin's letters, Bartram's travel journal, Weiser's later journal of 1748, a Moravian account of Count Zinzendorf's 1742 covenant, and the Virginia commissioners' journal of the Logstown council of 1752. Several of these are letters, minutes and deeds rather than diaries, and are tagged as such.

The heart of the chapter is the deed signed for Virginia on 2 July 1744. Virginia's commissioners asked for, and the chiefs signed, a release recognizing the King's right to all the lands within the colony; Virginia later read this as reaching to the Ohio under its sea-to-sea charter. Eight years later at Logstown a Haudenosaunee leader told Virginia's commissioners, as interpreted, that they had never understood the land sold to run west beyond the mountains. Both positions are set out here as the records give them.

Two later afterlives of the council are also recorded. Canasatego's closing advice of 4 July, that the colonies should unite as the Five Nations had, was printed by Franklin and echoed in his 1751 letter on colonial union; whether and how far the Haudenosaunee example shaped later American federal thought is debated by historians and is presented here only as dated statements. And the exchange of 3–4 July over educating Haudenosaunee boys in Virginia, which the minutes record in a few lines, became in Franklin's 1784 retelling a celebrated story with a counter-offer that the minutes do not contain.
calendar_note: The British colonies used the Julian (Old Style) calendar until September 1752, eleven days behind the Gregorian calendar in the 1740s; the legal year began on 25 March, which is why Franklin dated his letter to Parker '20 March 1750/1'. In this chapter date_iso keeps the dates exactly as the minutes, journals and letters give them (Old Style) for everything up to the Logstown council of June 1752, so 4 July 1744 in the minutes is 15 July 1744 in the Gregorian calendar; the New Style equivalent is shown in date_display. Moravian records were commonly kept in the New Style; the Zinzendorf entry is converted and marked approximate. Entries from 1753 onward are Gregorian, since Britain and its colonies changed calendars in September 1752.
vantage_key: 0 = principal speaker or negotiator at the council; 1 = present at Lancaster or the council in question as secretary, interpreter or guest; 2 = in Pennsylvania, near the council; 3 = elsewhere in the colonies; 4 = in Europe or writing years later.

eyes.name: Canasatego (Canassatego)
eyes.role: Onondaga (Onöñda'gega') sachem and chief speaker of the Haudenosaunee Grand Council; about sixty in 1744 by Marshe's estimate
eyes.where: Lancaster courthouse and the Haudenosaunee camp on the town's edge; Philadelphia in 1742
eyes.form: speeches (as interpreted by Conrad Weiser, in council minutes)
eyes.language: Onondaga (rendered into English by Conrad Weiser)
eyes.authenticity: No text in Canasatego's own hand or language survives. His speeches exist only in the English of the interpreter Conrad Weiser as taken down by the Pennsylvania secretary's office and printed by Franklin (1743 for the 1742 council, 1744 for Lancaster). Franklin's 1784 'Remarks Concerning the Savages of North America' attributes to the Lancaster speaker a fuller education speech that the 1744 minutes do not contain.
eyes.bio: Canasatego was the Confederacy's leading orator in its dealings with Pennsylvania in the 1740s and a firm ally of the Penn proprietors, which shaped his harsh rebuke of the Lenape in 1742. At Lancaster he negotiated land releases to Maryland and Virginia in return for goods and gold, while insisting on the Confederacy's conquest rights. His closing advice that the colonies unite as the Five Nations had done is the most quoted passage of the treaty.

sources.title: A Treaty, Held at the Town of Lancaster (1744), UNL Early Recognized Treaties edition
The Treaty Held with the Indians of the Six Nations at Philadelphia, in July 1742 (Project Gutenberg)

eyes.name: Tachanoontia
eyes.role: Onondaga chief and speaker at Lancaster; one of the signers of the Maryland deed (as 'Tacanuntie')
eyes.form: speech (as interpreted by Conrad Weiser, in council minutes)
eyes.language: Onondaga (rendered into English by Conrad Weiser)
eyes.authenticity: Known only through the printed minutes and the deed signatures; his reply to Virginia survives in Weiser's English.
eyes.bio: Tachanoontia gave the Confederacy's first answer to Virginia's claim that the Haudenosaunee had long since surrendered their lands to the King. His speech set out the right of conquest over the peoples of the Susquehanna and the lands beyond the Potomac's north branch, the argument Virginia's commissioners then disputed.

sources.title: A Treaty, Held at the Town of Lancaster (1744)
Maryland deed of 30 June 1744, Archives of Maryland vol. 700 p. 10

eyes.name: Gachradodow
eyes.role: Gayogo̱hó:nǫ' (Cayuga) chief, speaker for the Cayuga nation at Lancaster
eyes.form: speeches (as interpreted by Conrad Weiser, in council minutes)
eyes.language: Cayuga (rendered into English by Conrad Weiser)
eyes.authenticity: Known only through the printed minutes; his words survive in Weiser's English.
eyes.bio: Gachradodow answered Virginia on 30 June, reporting that the Catawba had refused peace and asking to see Virginia's goods before concluding. Chosen by lot, he conferred the name Tocarry-hogan on Maryland's absent proprietor at the dinner that evening, and on the last night the Maryland commissioners gave him a gold-laced hat.

sources.title: A Treaty, Held at the Town of Lancaster (1744)

eyes.name: Johann Conrad Weiser
eyes.role: Pennsylvania's official interpreter to the Six Nations, aged 47; farmer at Tulpehocken; lived among the Mohawk as a youth
eyes.side: Pennsylvania; trusted go-between for the Haudenosaunee
eyes.where: Lancaster; earlier at Onondaga (1743); later at Logstown on the Ohio (1748)
eyes.form: interpreter's renderings (in minutes), deed signature and dated journal (1748)
eyes.authenticity: Every Haudenosaunee speech in the Lancaster minutes passed through Weiser. His 1748 journal to the Ohio survives in an official copy printed in Pennsylvania Colonial Records vol. 5 and in a family copy printed in 1851; Thwaites reprinted it in Early Western Travels vol. 1 (1904).
eyes.bio: Raised partly among the Mohawk in New York, Weiser was the hinge on which Pennsylvania's Indian diplomacy turned in the 1740s; the Virginia and Maryland commissioners privately doubted his loyalty before the council. At Lancaster he advised the chiefs on valuing Maryland's goods, persuaded holdouts to sign, and signed for the absent Mohawks under his Haudenosaunee name. In 1748 he carried a joint Pennsylvania–Virginia present to the Ohio peoples at Logstown.

sources.title: Journals of Conrad Weiser (1748) and others, Early Western Travels vol. 1 (Project Gutenberg)
Conrad Weiser Homestead timeline
J. S. Walton, Conrad Weiser and the Indian Policy of Colonial Pennsylvania (1900)

eyes.name: Witham Marshe
eyes.role: Secretary to the Maryland commissioners, from Annapolis
eyes.where: Lancaster, lodging at Peter Worrall's inn on West King Street
eyes.authenticity: His 'Journal of the Treaty held with the Six Nations' was first printed in the Collections of the Massachusetts Historical Society, 1st series vol. 7 (1801), and reissued as 'Lancaster in 1744', ed. W. H. Egle (Lancaster, 1884). Passages here are taken from those printings as quoted in Walton (1900) and Heisey's Lancaster County Historical Society article.
eyes.bio: Marshe's journal is the only private, day-by-day account of the council, full of what the minutes leave out: the procession, the camp built of boughs, dances by firelight, a ball at which he mocked some of the town's women, and the dinner at which the chiefs heard huzzas for the first time. He was frankly partisan, crediting Weiser's 'dexterous management' for Maryland's deed and blaming Pennsylvania for the delays.

sources.title: Lancaster in 1744: Journal of the Treaty (1884), Library of Congress
M. Luther Heisey, 'The Indian Treaty of 1744', Lancaster County Historical Society
J. S. Walton, Conrad Weiser (1900), chapter VII

eyes.name: George Thomas
eyes.role: Deputy (lieutenant) governor of Pennsylvania 1738–1747, host and chair of the council
eyes.authenticity: His speeches are in the printed minutes of 1742 and 1744; as the minutes were kept by his own government's secretary, they are the record closest to him.
eyes.bio: A West Indian planter appointed by the Penns, Thomas acted at Lancaster as broker between the Confederacy and the two southern colonies, whose quarrels with the Haudenosaunee threatened Pennsylvania's frontier. He also used the council to press for justice over the killing of the trader John Armstrong and to ask the Confederacy to keep the French out of its country.

sources.title: A Treaty, Held at the Town of Lancaster (1744)
The Treaty Held … at Philadelphia, in July 1742

eyes.name: Thomas Lee (with William Beverley)
eyes.role: Virginia commissioners: Lee, of Stratford Hall, a member of the Governor's Council; Beverley, a planter and land speculator
eyes.where: Lancaster courthouse; Stratford Hall, Westmoreland County
eyes.form: speeches (in council minutes), deed and dated letters
eyes.authenticity: Their speeches are in the printed minutes; the Virginia deed of 2 July 1744 survives and was proved at Williamsburg on 25 October 1744. Lee's letters to Weiser of 1744–1748 are held by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
eyes.bio: Lee led Virginia's case that the Haudenosaunee had long ago surrendered their lands to the Crown and that Virginia held its charter by conquest. Three years after Lancaster he helped organize the Ohio Company, which sought half a million acres beyond the mountains, the lands whose status the Lancaster deed left in dispute.

sources.title: Virginia deed of 2 July 1744 (Jefferson's West, UNL)
Thomas Lee letter to Conrad Weiser, 1744 (HSP Digital Library)
Ohio Company (Virginia Places)

eyes.name: The Maryland commissioners (Edmund Jenings and colleagues)
eyes.role: Commissioners for the Province of Maryland, led by Edmund Jenings, with Philip Thomas, Robert King and Thomas Colvill
eyes.authenticity: Their speeches appear in the printed minutes; the deed of 30 June 1744 is entered in the Maryland council proceedings and provincial land records (Archives of Maryland vols. 28 and 700).
eyes.bio: Maryland came to buy out the Confederacy's claim to the lands its settlers already held west of the Susquehanna and north of the Potomac. Its commissioners offered £300 in currency and got, for goods valued at about £220, a release whose boundary was drawn to take in every Maryland settlement.

sources.title: Archives of Maryland vol. 28 p. 336 (deed of 30 June 1744)
Archives of Maryland vol. 700 p. 10

eyes.name: Richard Peters
eyes.role: Anglican clergyman, Secretary of the Pennsylvania land office and of the Province; attested the official minutes
eyes.authenticity: The printed minutes close 'A true Copy, compared by RICHARD PETERS, Secry.' The minutes are an official record shaped by Pennsylvania; Peters also witnessed the Maryland deed of 30 June.
eyes.bio: Peters ran the proprietors' land business, so the official account of Lancaster passed under the eye of the man most concerned with Pennsylvania's own land claims. His attested minutes, printed by Franklin, became the standard text of the council for colonists and historians alike.

sources.title: A Treaty, Held at the Town of Lancaster (1744)
Library of Congress copy of Franklin's 1744 printing

eyes.name: Benjamin Franklin
eyes.role: Philadelphia printer, aged 38 in 1744; later colonial agent and American minister in France
eyes.where: Philadelphia, his printing office near the Market; Passy, France, in 1783–84
eyes.form: dated letters, printed treaty and essay (written later)
eyes.authenticity: His letters to William Strahan (4 July and 18 September 1744) and to James Parker (20 March 1750/1) are edited in the Papers of Benjamin Franklin. 'Remarks Concerning the Savages of North America' was written before 7 January 1784 and printed at Passy in 1784; its Lancaster anecdote differs from the 1744 minutes, as the editors note.
eyes.bio: Franklin was not at Lancaster, but he printed its minutes, shipped them to London for sale, and carried Canasatego's advice on union into his own arguments for a colonial union in 1751. Forty years after the council he retold the education exchange in a form much more pointed than the minutes, in a satirical essay written in France.

eyes.name: John Bartram
eyes.role: Quaker farmer and botanist of Kingsessing near Philadelphia, aged 44 in 1743
eyes.where: On the road with Weiser to Onondaga and Oswego, July–August 1743
eyes.authenticity: Bartram sent his journal to Peter Collinson in London, who published it without Bartram having intended it for print as 'Observations on the Inhabitants, Climate, Soil, Rivers, Productions, Animals…' (London, 1751).
eyes.bio: Bartram rode north with Weiser and the surveyor Lewis Evans on the mission that prepared the way for Lancaster, observing plants, soils and the Onondaga town. His journal records an Onondaga longhouse some eighty feet long where the party lodged, and his sketch of it was printed with the book.

sources.title: John Bartram's Journey to Onondaga, 1743 (Bartram's Garden)
Observations… (London, 1751), Canadiana record

eyes.name: Nikolaus Ludwig, Count von Zinzendorf
eyes.role: Saxon nobleman and leader of the Moravian Church (Unitas Fratrum), visiting Pennsylvania 1741–1743
eyes.where: Tulpehocken, at Conrad Weiser's farm; Bethlehem
eyes.authenticity: His meeting with Six Nations deputies is recorded in Moravian sources summarized in J. M. Levering's History of Bethlehem (1903); Moravian dates were usually New Style. The exact form of the covenant is known only from the Moravian side.
eyes.bio: Zinzendorf met Haudenosaunee deputies at Weiser's farm in 1742, soon after the Philadelphia council, and made a covenant that his missionaries could travel among the Six Nations, receiving a wampum belt. His presence shows how many projects, religious as well as territorial, ran through Weiser and the Confederacy in the years before Lancaster.

sources.title: Levering, A History of Bethlehem, Pennsylvania (1903), part 18

eyes.name: Tanacharison (the 'Half King')
eyes.role: Seneca leader at Logstown on the Ohio, spokesman for the Haudenosaunee there in the 1750s
eyes.form: speech (as interpreted, in Virginia commissioners' journal)
eyes.language: Seneca (interpreted into English; Andrew Montour served as interpreter at the council)
eyes.authenticity: His words survive in the journal of the Virginia commissioners Joshua Fry, Lunsford Lomax and James Patton at Logstown, 1752, printed in the Virginia Magazine of History and Biography (1906). The journal names Montour as interpreter for the sessions without assigning each speech.
eyes.bio: Tanacharison was the Haudenosaunee voice on the upper Ohio in the years when Virginia's Ohio Company sought to settle there. At Logstown he told Virginia's commissioners that the Confederacy had not understood the Lancaster sale to reach so far west, then agreed to confirm the deed and allow settlement south-east of the Ohio.

sources.title: Treaty of Logstown, 1752: Virginia commissioners' journal (UNL)

entries.headline: Canasatego complains of settlers from the south
entries.digest: Answering Governor Thomas at the Philadelphia council, Canasatego (as Weiser interpreted him) complained that people from the colonies to the south were settling lands west of the Susquehanna that the Confederacy had never sold. He wanted those lands paid for. The complaint became the seed of the Lancaster council two years later.
entries.source_note: The Treaty Held with the Indians of the Six Nations at Philadelphia, in July 1742 (London reprint), Six Nations' answer of 7 July; the Maryland complaint is recorded in the 1742 minutes, day of the specific passage approximate. https://gutenberg.org/files/18635/18635-h/18635-h.htm

entries.headline: Pennsylvania's council agrees to write to Maryland
entries.digest: After the Six Nations' answer, the Pennsylvania council resolved to make the chiefs a present and to write to the Governor of Maryland asking for a satisfactory answer about the settlers. The present was delivered at the Great Meeting-House on 10 July. Pennsylvania thus took on the role of go-between that it would play at Lancaster.
entries.source_note: 1742 treaty minutes, councils of 8 and 10 July. https://gutenberg.org/files/18635/18635-h/18635-h.htm

entries.headline: Canasatego orders the Lenape off the Forks
entries.digest: At a council in the Proprietor's house, Canasatego, interpreted by Weiser, scolded the Lenape (Delaware) leaders from the Forks of the Delaware and ordered them to leave lands Pennsylvania claimed under its disputed 1737 Walking Purchase. He claimed the Lenape as a people conquered by the Confederacy who had no right to sell land, using a gendered insult the minutes record. Lenape leaders protested the removal in a petition that November.
entries.source_note: 1742 treaty minutes, council of 12 July. https://gutenberg.org/files/18635/18635-h/18635-h.htm ; Walton (1900) on the November 1742 petition. https://distantreader.org/stacks/trust/uc2/uc2_ark+=13960=t6xw48596.txt

entries.date_display: 3 August 1742 as given in the Moravian record (probably N.S.; c. 23 July O.S.)
entries.headline: Zinzendorf's covenant with Six Nations deputies
entries.digest: Count Zinzendorf met representatives of the Six Nations at Weiser's farm and made a covenant allowing his Moravian brethren to travel among them, receiving a wampum belt. He gave the chiefs a seal so they could recognize his messengers. The belt went with him to England and came back to Pennsylvania with Spangenberg in 1743.
entries.source_note: Levering, History of Bethlehem (1903), summarizing Moravian records; calendar style not stated in the source. https://ldsgenealogy.com/PA/books/A-history-of-Bethlehem-Pennsylvania-1741-1892-with-some-account-of-its-founders-and-their-early-activity-in-America-part-18.htm

entries.headline: Bartram sets out north with the interpreter
entries.digest: Bartram left Philadelphia with Conrad Weiser and the surveyor Lewis Evans on Weiser's mission to Onondaga. The errand was Virginia's: to make peace after a Haudenosaunee war party and Virginia settlers had clashed in the Shenandoah Valley the previous December, with deaths on both sides. At Shamokin the party picked up the Oneida leader Shikellamy and his son as escorts.
entries.source_note: Bartram's Garden, 'John Bartram's Journey to Onondaga, 1743'. https://www.bartramsgarden.org/john-bartrams-journey-to-onondaga-1743/

entries.headline: Arrival at Onondaga and the long house
entries.digest: The party reached the Onondaga town, the seat of the Confederacy's council fire. Bartram recorded that they were lodged in a longhouse about eighty feet long, kept for ceremonial and diplomatic business, and later sketched it for his book. He went on to Oswego with Evans while Weiser negotiated.
entries.source_note: Bartram's Garden article on the 1743 journey. https://www.bartramsgarden.org/john-bartrams-journey-to-onondaga-1743/

entries.headline: Weiser carries Virginia's peace to the council fire
entries.digest: At Onondaga Weiser delivered Virginia's message after the Shenandoah clash, and the proceedings ended in peace, with the Confederacy's land grievances against Virginia and Maryland left for a larger meeting. Bartram and Evans returned from Oswego on 27 July in time for the final days of the council. That larger meeting became Lancaster.
entries.source_note: Bartram's Garden article (return 27 July; peace concluded); Weiser's own 1743 journal is printed in the Pennsylvania records but was not consulted here. https://www.bartramsgarden.org/john-bartrams-journey-to-onondaga-1743/

entries.headline: Home, with a journal not meant for print
entries.digest: Bartram was back in Philadelphia by 19 August. He sent his journal to his London correspondent Peter Collinson, who published it in 1751 with Bartram's sketch of Oswego and the Onondaga longhouse, though Bartram had not written it for the public.
entries.source_note: Bartram's Garden article. https://www.bartramsgarden.org/john-bartrams-journey-to-onondaga-1743/

entries.place: Lancaster courthouse and the town's edge
entries.headline: The procession arrives while the commissioners dine
entries.digest: Marshe and the commissioners were at dinner in the courthouse, a two-storey brick building he thought could hold above eight hundred people, when the Haudenosaunee deputies came in procession, conducted by Weiser to their camp. The camp stood on vacant lots at the edge of town, with cabins of boughs set out by rank, the Onondaga first. Weiser asked the townspeople not to talk much about the visitors or mock their dress.
entries.quote: a pretty large brick building two stories high
entries.source_note: Marshe's journal as quoted in Heisey, 'The Indian Treaty of 1744' and Walton (1900). https://collections.lancasterhistory.org/media/library/docs/edit_vol48no3pp57_70.pdf

entries.headline: Governor Thomas opens the council
entries.digest: In the courthouse Governor Thomas, with the Virginia and Maryland commissioners beside him, welcomed the Six Nations deputies; Canasatego and Tachanoontia replied. Thomas proposed that business begin on Monday, after the deputies had rested from their journey.
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, session of 22 June. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: A Sabbath at Ephrata and a dance by firelight
entries.digest: The governor and commissioners rode out to the Seventh Day Baptist community at Ephrata, it being their Sabbath. Back in Lancaster, Marshe watched thirty or forty young Haudenosaunee men form a ring around a fire while three older men drummed and sang, the dancers hopping and calling out for hours. He admired them as agile, strong and straight-limbed.
entries.quote: surprisingly agile, strong and straight-limbed
entries.source_note: Marshe's journal as quoted in Walton (1900), ch. VII; the day of the dance follows Walton's placement after the Ephrata visit. https://distantreader.org/stacks/trust/uc2/uc2_ark+=13960=t6xw48596.txt

entries.headline: Thomas lays out the land quarrel
entries.digest: Thomas explained the dispute: the Confederacy said Maryland's settlers held land without its consent or any purchase, and Virginia's quarrel had already turned bloody. He urged the deputies to settle peacefully with both colonies, and Maryland's commissioners spoke after him. Canasatego replied that the Virginia and Maryland disputes should be settled first.
entries.quote: without their Consent, or any Purchase made from them
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 25 June A.M. and P.M. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: Canasatego tells the history of the chain
entries.digest: Answering Maryland, Canasatego, as Weiser rendered him, went back to the coming of the Dutch: a ship tied first with a rope, then with stronger bonds, and finally with a silver chain under the English. He said New York's governor had taken the Susquehanna lands into his keeping and sold them to the Penns. The history was an argument: the Confederacy had been the land's owner from the start.
entries.quote: a Silver Chain, which would be much stronger
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 26 June P.M. (speech as interpreted by Conrad Weiser). https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: Virginia says the land was already the King's
entries.digest: Speaking for Assaragoa, as the Haudenosaunee called Virginia's governor, the commissioners declared that the Six Nations had long ago given up their lands to the Great King and that Virginia had been held under the Crown for over 160 years. They allowed there might be a mistake, proposed asking New York's governor to look into it, and offered a chest of new goods.
entries.quote: you had given up your Lands to the Great King
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 27 June A.M. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: Tachanoontia answers with the right of conquest
entries.digest: In the afternoon Tachanoontia, as interpreted by Weiser, rejected Virginia's claim. The Confederacy held the peoples beyond the Susquehanna and the north branch of the Potomac by conquest, he said, and had never given that right up. He also raised the road agreed at Albany, which he said Virginians had ignored.
entries.quote: All the World knows we conquered
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 27 June P.M. (speech as interpreted). https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: A ball, and a secretary's sharp eye
entries.digest: James Hamilton gave a ball for the visiting gentlemen. Marshe made fun of two of the local women, writing that they danced wilder than any Indians, and praised some Jewish women of the town as well dressed and agreeable. His jokes show the colonial company relaxing while the land argument went on in the courthouse.
entries.source_note: Marshe's journal as quoted in Heisey, 'The Indian Treaty of 1744'. https://collections.lancasterhistory.org/media/library/docs/edit_vol48no3pp57_70.pdf

entries.headline: A murdered trader and a demand for justice
entries.digest: Thomas told the deputies that three Lenape men had killed the trader John Armstrong and his two servants and taken his goods. He asked the Confederacy, which claimed authority over the Lenape, to secure the two suspects still at large and recover the goods for the widows and children, and backed the request with a string of wampum.
entries.quote: three of the Delaware Indians lately murdered
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 28 June A.M. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: Maryland puts £300 on the table
entries.digest: The Maryland commissioners offered £300 in currency for a release of the Confederacy's claims. The deputies chose goods instead, valued at £220 15s Pennsylvania currency; Marshe credited Weiser with advising them on the valuation.
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 28 June P.M.; Walton (1900) on Weiser's advice. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: Virginia answers conquest with conquest
entries.digest: Virginia's speaker replied that the Great King held Virginia by right of conquest, that the lands beyond the mountains had lain deserted and had never been held by the Six Nations, and cited earlier Albany treaties and Governor Spotswood's agreement. Yet the commissioners added that Virginia would pay for any rights the Confederacy could show, and offered terms on the road south.
entries.quote: the Great King holds Virginia by Right of Conquest
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 28 June P.M. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: A map drawn for Lord Baltimore
entries.digest: Using a drawing of the Potomac and the Susquehanna, Canasatego offered Maryland a release of rights north of the Potomac. He proposed lines that would take in all Maryland's existing settlements and asked that settlers beyond them be accepted as brothers. Weiser rendered the offer in English.
entries.quote: We are willing to renounce all Right to Lord Baltimore
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 29 June A.M. (speech as interpreted). https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: The Cayuga speaker questions Virginia's case
entries.digest: Gachradodow, speaking for the Cayuga, answered Virginia's conquest argument and questioned its justice. He reported that the Catawba had refused the peace Virginia had urged and said the deputies wished to see Virginia's goods before they concluded anything. The speech survives in Weiser's English.
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 30 June A.M. (speech as interpreted). https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: A name for Maryland's absent proprietor
entries.digest: At the dinner the three colonies gave the chiefs, Gachradodow, chosen by lot for the task, conferred a name on Lord Baltimore, who had never been to America. The minutes give it as Tocarry-hogan; Marshe recorded it as a name signifying a fine place between Assaragoa (Virginia) and Onas (Pennsylvania).
entries.quote: they had agreed to give him the Name of Tocarry-hogan
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 30 June P.M.; Walton (1900) on Marshe's gloss. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: Huzzas the chiefs had never heard
entries.digest: Marshe noted that twenty-four chiefs dined at five tables with the commissioners and townspeople, used no forks, and seemed hugely pleased with the feast. When the company gave three huzzas after the naming, the noise startled them. When the deed was brought out, the Oneida leader Shikellamy objected and the business stalled for the day, which Marshe blamed on underhanded dealing by Pennsylvania.
entries.quote: seemed prodigiously pleased with their feast
entries.source_note: Marshe's journal as quoted in Walton (1900), ch. VII. https://distantreader.org/stacks/trust/uc2/uc2_ark+=13960=t6xw48596.txt

entries.headline: The Maryland deed is executed
entries.digest: The minutes record that Canasatego and thirteen other chiefs executed the deed to Maryland that day; Peters signed among the witnesses, with Weiser as interpreter. The deed released the Confederacy's claims within lines running north to the Pennsylvania boundary and then to the Susquehanna, stretched where necessary so that every Maryland settler fell inside.
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 30 June P.M.; deed text in Archives of Maryland vol. 28 p. 336 and vol. 700 p. 10. https://msa.maryland.gov/megafile/msa/speccol/sc2900/sc2908/000001/000028/html/am28--336.html

entries.headline: Maryland's purchase completed at Sanderson's
entries.digest: At Sanderson's inn the remaining chiefs signed the Maryland deed, and Canasatego and some sixteen sachems delivered it. Marshe celebrated the purchase of some hundred thousand acres for Lord Baltimore and gave the credit to the interpreter. Shikellamy, by Walton's account, never signed.
entries.quote: by the dexterous management of the interpreter
entries.source_note: Marshe's journal as quoted in Walton (1900); printed minutes, 2 July A.M. at Sanderson's. https://distantreader.org/stacks/trust/uc2/uc2_ark+=13960=t6xw48596.txt

entries.headline: The interpreter signs for the absent Mohawk
entries.digest: With no Kanien'kehá:ka (Mohawk) delegation at Lancaster, Weiser signed the Maryland deed on their behalf under his Haudenosaunee name, Tarachiawagon, rendered as Holder of the Heavens, and witnessed it as interpreter. The same man was thus translator, witness and signatory.
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 2 July A.M.; Conrad Weiser Homestead timeline; Walton (1900). https://conradweiserhomestead.org/timeline/

entries.headline: Canasatego answers on the Armstrong killing
entries.digest: Canasatego, through Weiser, agreed that the killing of Armstrong had to be answered: the Confederacy would reprove the Lenape, who were under its power, send the suspects for examination and search again for the stolen goods. He also asked Pennsylvania to help the Piscataway (Conoy), who wished to move to Shamokin.
entries.quote: are under our Power
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 2 July A.M. (speech as interpreted). https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: The Virginia deed: the King's right to all the lands
entries.digest: Virginia offered goods worth £200 in Pennsylvania money and £200 in gold, on condition that the chiefs first sign a deed recognizing the King's right to all the lands in the colony. The deed was executed by Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca chiefs, for £400 in all; Canasatego asked that the Confederacy's own petition be sent to the King, and the commissioners promised to forward it. Rum was given for the journey home.
entries.quote: a Deed recognizing the King's Right to all the Lands
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 2 July P.M.; Virginia deed text (Jefferson's West). https://jeffersonswest.unl.edu/archive/view_doc_jef.00083.html

entries.headline: News of war with France
entries.digest: Thomas told the deputies that Britain and France were at war, that two battles had already been fought, and asked the Confederacy to honour its treaties, keep the French out of its country and pass on intelligence. Virginia and Maryland each added £100 in gold, and Pennsylvania goods worth £300.
entries.quote: Two Battles have been fought, one by Land
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 3 July A.M. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: An invitation to send boys to Virginia
entries.digest: In the same morning's speeches the Virginia commissioners invited the Six Nations to send three or four of their boys to Virginia to be educated. The minutes give the offer in a single passage, with none of the detail of the later retelling.
entries.quote: three or four of your Boys to Virginia
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 3 July A.M. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: Unite, as our forefathers did
entries.digest: In his closing answer to the three governments, Canasatego, interpreted by Weiser, promised to keep the French out of the Confederacy's country and spoke of the Catawba war. He then advised the colonies to keep union among themselves as the Five Nations' forefathers had done: union had made the Confederacy formidable and would give the colonies fresh strength, so they should never fall out with one another.
entries.quote: OUR wise Forefathers established Union and Amity
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 4 July A.M. (speech as interpreted by Conrad Weiser). https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: The education offer declined in a sentence
entries.digest: In the Six Nations' replies that morning, addressed to Assaragoa, the deputies declined Virginia's invitation: they loved their children too much to send them so far, and Haudenosaunee people were not inclined to give their children that kind of learning. The minutes do not name the speaker at this point; Canasatego was the principal speaker that morning. There is no counter-offer in the 1744 text.
entries.quote: we love our Children too well
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, 4 July A.M. (as interpreted). https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: Franklin mentions the treaty in a business letter
entries.digest: On the same day that Canasatego spoke, Franklin wrote to his London friend William Strahan about type, pamphlets and colonial news, mentioning that a treaty was being held in Lancaster County between Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania and the united Five Nations. He promised an account once it was printed, referring to the Haudenosaunee with a dismissive term common among colonists.
entries.source_note: Franklin to William Strahan, 4 July 1744, Papers of Benjamin Franklin vol. 2. https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Franklin/01-02-02-0106

entries.headline: Huzzas, a coat, a hat and a string about a beard
entries.digest: The council closed with a toast to the King and the Six Nations and three huzzas. That evening the governor gave farewell wampum, including a string concerning Conrad Weiser's beard; Virginia gave Canasatego a scarlet camlet coat and Maryland gave Gachradodow a gold-laced hat. Peters attested the minutes as a true copy.
entries.source_note: Printed minutes, close of 4 July; attestation by Richard Peters. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00003.html

entries.headline: The treaty goes on sale
entries.digest: The Pennsylvania Gazette advertised Franklin's printing of the Lancaster minutes at eighteen pence. The folio carried the speeches of Canasatego, Tachanoontia and Gachradodow to colonial readers in Weiser's English.
entries.source_note: Editors' note to Franklin to Strahan, 18 September 1744 (Gazette advertisement of 6 September). https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Franklin/01-02-02-0111

entries.headline: Two hundred copies for London
entries.digest: Franklin sent Strahan 200 copies of the treaty, hoping they would sell in London and offering to take books in exchange for whatever sold. The council's minutes thus became a commercial publication on both sides of the Atlantic.
entries.source_note: Franklin to William Strahan, 18 September 1744. https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Franklin/01-02-02-0111

entries.headline: The Virginia deed recorded at Williamsburg
entries.digest: The deed Lee and Beverley brought home, signed for the Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, was proved at the General Court in the Capitol at Williamsburg and ordered recorded. In it the chiefs renounced claims to land in the colony and acknowledged the King's right to it, for £400 Pennsylvania currency paid in goods and gold.
entries.source_note: Virginia deed poll of 2 July 1744 with its certificate of proof (Jefferson's West, UNL). https://jeffersonswest.unl.edu/archive/view_doc_jef.00083.html

entries.headline: Weiser reaches Logstown
entries.digest: Weiser had set out from his house on 11 August with a joint present from Pennsylvania and Virginia, Virginia contributing £200. He reached Logstown on the Ohio in the evening of 27 August and was greeted with a salute. On 8 September he recorded the fighting men each nation reported, 789 in all, Delawares, Seneca and Shawnee the most numerous.
entries.source_note: Weiser's 1748 journal, Early Western Travels vol. 1 (Project Gutenberg). https://gutenberg.org/files/73714/73714-h/73714-h.htm

entries.headline: The present divided in five shares
entries.digest: At the formal council Weiser divided the goods into five shares, one for each group of nations gathered on the Ohio, and spoke of arrangements announced at 'the last Treaty in Lancaster'. He left in the rain on 19 September. Four years later the Ohio Seneca would recall these goods as having come from Pennsylvania rather than the King.
entries.source_note: Weiser's 1748 journal; Logstown journal of 1752 for the later recollection. https://gutenberg.org/files/73714/73714-h/73714-h.htm

entries.headline: Franklin turns the union advice into a plan
entries.digest: Commenting on Archibald Kennedy's pamphlet on Indian affairs, Franklin argued that if the Six Nations could form a union that had lasted for ages, ten or a dozen English colonies needing it more should manage one too. He proposed a voluntary general council funded by an excise on liquor. The letter, printed in Kennedy's pamphlet in 1751, also contains a disparaging phrase about the Six Nations.
entries.quote: it has subsisted Ages, and appears indissoluble
entries.source_note: Franklin to James Parker, 20 March 1751, Papers of Benjamin Franklin vol. 4. https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Franklin/01-04-02-0037

entries.headline: 'We never understood'
entries.digest: A day after Virginia's commissioners explained what they took the Lancaster deed to cover, Tanacharison replied, as interpreted, that the Confederacy had never understood the lands then sold to run further toward the setting sun than the hill on the far side of the Allegheny ridge. He set the Haudenosaunee reading of the 1744 deed directly against Virginia's.
entries.quote: the Lands then sold were to extend further to the Sun setting
entries.source_note: Virginia commissioners' journal of the Logstown council, 11 June 1752 (speech as interpreted; Andrew Montour interpreter for the sessions). https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00004.html

entries.headline: The Lancaster deed confirmed, with settlement allowed
entries.digest: Two days later the Haudenosaunee leaders at Logstown signed an instrument confirming the Lancaster deed and consenting to British settlement on the south-east side of the Ohio. The Virginia commissioners recorded it as settling the question; within two years the upper Ohio was the opening ground of the war with France.
entries.source_note: Logstown journal and instrument dated 13 June 1752. https://treatiesportal.unl.edu/earlytreaties/treaty.00004.html

entries.headline: A first telling of the education story
entries.digest: Writing to Peter Collinson, Franklin told a story about the Lancaster education offer, an earlier and shorter version of the anecdote he would publish in 1784. The editors of his papers note that both versions differ from the official record of 1744.
entries.source_note: Known here from the editors' note to 'Remarks concerning the Savages of North America', which cites Franklin to Collinson, 9 May 1753. https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Franklin/01-41-02-0280

entries.headline: Franklin's Lancaster story, forty years on
entries.digest: In his satirical 'Remarks Concerning the Savages of North America', Franklin told how Virginia offered places at the Williamsburg college for half a dozen Haudenosaunee sons, and how the speaker, after a day's reflection, declined: youths educated in the northern colleges came home unable to hunt, build or endure hardship. He added a counter-offer, absent from the 1744 minutes, to take a dozen Virginian sons and educate them in turn.
entries.quote: make Men of them
entries.source_note: Remarks concerning the Savages of North America (before 7 January 1784), Papers of Benjamin Franklin vol. 41, with editors' notes. https://founders.archives.gov/documents/Franklin/01-41-02-0280

claims.claim: Settlers from the south hold Haudenosaunee land west of the Susquehanna without purchase and must pay for it
The Lenape at the Forks must leave the lands Pennsylvania bought; as a conquered people they had no right to sell
The Confederacy says Maryland's lands were settled without its consent or any purchase; the dispute should be settled peaceably
claims.evidence: A Treaty, Held at the Town of Lancaster, 25 June A.M.

claims.claim: The Six Nations long ago gave up their lands to the Great King; Virginia has been held under the Crown for over 160 years
The Confederacy holds the lands beyond the Susquehanna and the Potomac's north branch by right of conquest and never relinquished it
The King holds Virginia by conquest and the lands beyond the mountains were never held by the Six Nations, yet Virginia will pay for any rights shown
Maryland offers £300 currency for a release of claims; goods accepted at £220 15s
The Confederacy will renounce its rights north of the Potomac to Lord Baltimore, within lines taking in all Maryland settlers
Deed: Six Nations release lands within Maryland's lines; settlers outside the lines may stay in peaceable possession as brethren
claims.evidence: Maryland deed of 30 June 1744, Archives of Maryland vols. 28 and 700

claims.claim: Deed: the chiefs renounce claims to land in the colony of Virginia and recognize the King's right to all of it, for £400
claims.evidence: Virginia deed poll of 2 July 1744, proved 25 October 1744

claims.claim: The Confederacy asks that its own petition be laid before the King; Virginia promises to forward it
Virginia invites the Six Nations to send three or four boys to Virginia for education
The colonies should keep union with one another as the Five Nations' forefathers did, and so gain strength
The Six Nations decline to send their children so far for schooling
claims.evidence: Printed minutes, 4 July A.M. (speaker not named at this passage)

claims.claim: The Confederacy never understood the Lancaster sale to reach further west than the hill beyond the Allegheny ridge
The Lancaster speaker declined Virginia's college offer and proposed instead to educate a dozen Virginian sons
claims.evidence: Franklin, 'Remarks Concerning the Savages of North America' (Passy, 1784); not in the 1744 minutes

convergences.label: Philadelphia council and Zinzendorf's covenant, July 1742
convergences.note: Within a fortnight the same Haudenosaunee leaders who backed Pennsylvania against the Lenape at Philadelphia met a Moravian count at Weiser's farm: land and missions ran through the same interpreter and the same council fire.

convergences.label: Weiser and Bartram at Onondaga
convergences.note: The diplomat negotiated peace after the Shenandoah clash while the botanist measured the longhouse and went botanizing toward Oswego; one record is of politics, the other of plants, soil and buildings.

convergences.label: The deputies arrive at Lancaster
convergences.note: The minutes record a formal welcome and an adjournment to Monday; Marshe records the procession interrupting dinner, the camp of boughs and Weiser's request that the townspeople not mock their guests.

convergences.label: Virginia's claim, the conquest answer, and a ball
convergences.note: In the courthouse two claims of conquest met head-on; in the evening the same colonial company danced at James Hamilton's ball, and Marshe's journal turns from treaty to gossip.

convergences.label: Dinner, naming and the Maryland deed
convergences.note: The minutes record the name Tocarry-hogan and fourteen signatures; Marshe records the forks, the startled reaction to the huzzas, and Shikellamy's objection that held the deed up, blaming Pennsylvania.

convergences.label: The two deeds signed
convergences.note: Maryland's deed was completed at Sanderson's, with Weiser signing for the absent Mohawk; that afternoon Virginia's deed recognized the King's right to all the colony's lands, the wording later read so differently in Virginia and at Logstown.

convergences.label: Union advice in Lancaster; a business letter in Philadelphia
convergences.note: As Canasatego urged the colonies to unite, Franklin, sixty miles away, mentioned the treaty in a letter to London in dismissive terms; within seven years he would use the Confederacy's union as his model in arguing for a colonial one.

ties.note: Weiser rendered every speech Canasatego gave at Philadelphia in 1742 and Lancaster in 1744; Canasatego's words reach us only through him.
Marshe credited Maryland's deed to Weiser's 'dexterous management', though the Maryland and Virginia commissioners had privately doubted Weiser's reliability in May 1744.
They travelled together to Onondaga in July 1743 on the mission that led to Lancaster.
Philadelphia friends and correspondents of the London merchant Peter Collinson; Collinson published Bartram's journal in 1751 and received Franklin's first telling of the education story in 1753.
Franklin printed Canasatego's speeches in 1743 and 1744 and adapted his advice on union in 1751; he never met him, as far as the sources here show.
Peters attested the official minutes; Franklin printed and sold them in Philadelphia and London.
Lee's Virginia claimed the land by the King's right and conquest; Tachanoontia claimed it by the Confederacy's conquest.
Gachradodow answered Virginia's conquest argument on 30 June and questioned its justice before the Virginia deed was signed.
Lee's Ohio Company depended on Virginia's broad reading of the 1744 deed; Tanacharison stated the narrower Haudenosaunee understanding at Logstown in 1752, two years after Lee's death.
Weiser delivered the 1748 present at Logstown; in 1752 the Half King recalled it as Pennsylvania's gift and dismissed Weiser's earlier assurances.
Zinzendorf's 1742 covenant with Six Nations deputies was made at Weiser's farm, and Weiser travelled with him into the Wyoming Valley that autumn.
They faced each other across the council table in Philadelphia in 1742 and at Lancaster in 1744, allies in Pennsylvania's dealings with the Lenape.

threads_out.note: Franklin printed Canasatego's 1744 union advice and in 1751 held up the Confederacy's union as a model for the colonies; he later sat in the Philadelphia Convention of 1787. How far the Haudenosaunee example shaped the federal Constitution is debated by historians; in October 1988 the US Congress passed a concurrent resolution acknowledging the Confederacy's influence.
The Ohio lands whose status the Lancaster deed left disputed, argued again at Logstown in 1752, became the war-torn ground ceded by the Western Confederacy nations at Greenville in 1795.

Franklin wrote his 'Remarks Concerning the Savages of North America', with its retelling of the Lancaster education exchange, at Passy in the winter of 1783–84, in the same months he was watching and writing about the first balloon ascents in Paris.
